title: What Hallucinations Have We Measured? Semantic Illusion, Confabulation, and Expressed Uncertainty

paper.title: What Hallucinations Have We Measured? Semantic Illusion, Confabulation, and Expressed Uncertainty
paper.abstract:
Abstract Hallucination remains one of the most critical challenges in deploying large language models (LLMs) reliably and safely.
Yet the term is used inconsistently across the research community.
We argue for a strict definition of hallucinations in LLMs.
First, hallucinations should be confident incorrectness , kept separate from expressed uncertainty ( unk ) 1 1 1 Model responses that explicitly communicate epistemic uncertainty, including both abstention (i.e., declining to provide an answer) and low-confidence answers (e.g., ”I am not sure but maybe …”, ”I don’t know but …”). . unk reveals that the model may be wrong, whereas a hallucination does not reveal it and is therefore more dangerous in practice. Conflating the two obscures their distinct behaviors and makes them hard to study.
Second, hallucinations should be split by a simple re-elicitation test: does any semantically equivalent prompt recover the correct response?
This test probes whether the relevant knowledge 2 2 2 We use knowledge loosely to mean relevant information stored in the model’s latent representations (i.e., pretrained, parametric knowledge). Whether a model truly possesses a piece of knowledge cannot be verified from the outside: it may be stored but unretrievable, or absent from training. We therefore operationally treat knowledge as accessible if some semantically equivalent prompt elicits it without model parameter changes. is accessible.
If none does, the knowledge is likely absent or inaccessible, and the error type is a confabulation ( cf ) that likely requires external knowledge or retraining; if some does, the knowledge is accessible from the model but applied inconsistently, and the error type is a semantic illusion ( si ) that simple prompt or decoding changes can mitigate 3 3 3 Any intervention that revises an originally incorrect model response into a correct one. .
Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods under this taxonomy yields three findings.
(1) Detection methods flag unk more often than hallucinated responses (i.e., si and cf ).
(2) Mitigation methods are far more effective for si than for cf .
(3) Latent signals are more informative than output-level signals for cf .
An audit of recent hallucination papers shows that most conflate these categories.
We recommend reporting cf , si , and unk separately, and introduce a practical labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of semantically equivalent prompts.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Original prompt answered correctly? Any re-elicitation answered correctly? Expresses uncertainty under any condition? No hallucination correct under the original prompt Semantic illusion hallucination, recoverable Expressed uncertainty admits it is unsure; not a hallucination Confabulation hallucination, unrecoverable yes yes yes no no no Re-elicitation: paraphrase, instruction or decoding change (without additional information) Figure 1: Proposed taxonomy of model responses. An incorrect answer is a semantic illusion if any semantically equivalent re-elicitation recovers the correct answer. If none does, it is a confabulation, unless the model expresses uncertainty under some condition, in which case it is unk . Only si and cf are hallucinations. Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a central concern for both researchers and practitioners. Yet there is surprisingly little consensus on what the term actually means. Across the literature, it is applied to a broad and heterogeneous set of model failures—factual inaccuracies [ 82 , 3 , 2 ] , faithfulness errors [ 45 , 117 ] , reasoning inconsistencies [ 39 , 12 ] , and uncertain outputs [ 117 , 39 , 102 ] —often without distinction or explicit definition. This conceptual ambiguity is not merely terminological but obscures the underlying causes of model incorrect responses, undermines evaluation validity, and hinders the development of targeted mitigation strategies. We propose one definition and one test (Fig. 1 ). A hallucination is a confident incorrect response, so a model that says “I don’t know” is expressing uncertainty ( unk ), not hallucinating. Hallucinations then split by whether the knowledge is behaviorally accessible . If some paraphrase, instruction or decoding setting recovers the correct answer, the error is a semantic illusion ( si ); if none does, it is a confabulation ( cf ) (see § 4 for terminological motivations). The test is an operational proxy for knowledge accessibility, and it makes a sharp prediction that si should yield to inexpensive inference-time mitigation, while cf should need new, additional knowledge. Our main contributions and findings are as follows: • An audit of the community (§ 3 ). Only 35% of recent hallucination papers define hallucination as confident incorrectness. Yet 95.8% of surveyed first authors say it should be distinguished from uncertainty, and only 16.7% report that they did so. • A behavioral taxonomy (§ 5 ) We define hallucination as a confidently incorrect response, separate from expressed uncertainty ( unk ), and introduce two error types based on a re-elicitation test: semantic illusions ( si ), which some semantically equivalent re-elicitation corrects, and confabulations ( cf ), which none does. We use this taxonomy to re-evaluate 14 hallucination methods on two LLMs. • Mitigation for semantic illusions, not for confabulations (§ 7 ). Methods mitigate 28–29% of detected si responses but 0.7–2.8% of cf responses; only external knowledge improves cf mitigation, to about 20%. • Uncertainty-based detectors mostly measure expressed uncertainty (§ 8 ). They give their highest scores to unk , which is not a hallucination, above both si and cf , and they miss half of the cf responses that remain once uncertainty is elicited. • The right uncertainty representation depends on the error type (§ 9 ). Among uncertainty representations, verbal ones detect unk best but barely mitigate it; latent ones detect and mitigate cf best; and semantic ones mitigate si best. These effects are invisible in an aggregate hallucination score. An audit of recent papers (§ 3 and § B ) shows such aggregation is the norm. We also contribute a labeling protocol (§ 5 ) that stabilizes at about ten paraphrases, so the taxonomy is plausible to adopt.

sections.heading: 2 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We formalize the two central hallucination dimensions – incorrectness and plausibility – through the following research questions (RQ). The detailed hypotheses (H) are illustrated in § E .

sections.heading: 2.1 RQ1 (Incorrectness): Do hallucinations arise from distinct error types?
sections.text: The most basic condition for hallucinations is incorrectness, whether measured against a source [ 45 , 117 ] , the real-world facts [ 82 , 3 , 2 ] , or an instruction [ 39 , 12 ] . Incorrect outputs, however, are not uniform in how they arise or how they respond to elicitation. Accordingly, the difference that matters most in practice is consistency of occurrence. Yet some incorrect responses can be corrected under a semantically equivalent phrasing ( semantic illusion ), while others recur whatever phrasing is used ( confabulation ) (see § 4 or § D for an explanation of the terminology). We ask whether these reflect distinct error types, and whether that distinction changes which detection and mitigation strategies apply. The difference also invites an epistemic reading, since a response that becomes correct under a semantically equivalent phrasing shows the relevant knowledge is accessible without changing model weights or injecting additional information. We therefore treat knowledge as behaviorally accessible when some tested condition elicits a correct response. The conditions we admit that establish accessibility are semantically equivalent phrasings, instruction variants, decoding configurations (e.g., temperature, nucleus sampling), which require no access to model internals and add no additional hints or context.

sections.heading: 2.2 RQ2 (Plausibility): Does hallucination require confident incorrectness?
sections.text: We define plausibility as confidence, because (i) current LLMs are fluent by default, so surface plausibility is satisfied by nearly every output and draws no useful boundary, and (ii) a confidently stated incorrect response gives the reader no cue to check it, which makes it the more dangerous error. We say a response is confident if it does not explicitly express uncertainty. A confidently incorrect response ( cf , si ) and an expressed uncertainty ( unk ) may both be scored as incorrect, but reflect qualitatively different behaviors and risks. Uncertainty estimation methods were originally developed to quantify epistemic uncertainty as a signal for detecting incorrect outputs, whereas unk is a behavior in which the model explicitly abstains or gives a low-confidence answer. As LLMs increasingly exhibit this behavior, the remaining errors are predominantly confident ones, where output-level uncertainty signals have least to detect. We ask whether confidence is a necessary condition for hallucination and whether existing methods respect this distinction in practice.

sections.heading: 3 What the Community Measures
sections.text: Figure 2: Recent text-based hallucination papers filtered by their definitions and approaches with uncertainty estimation, additional knowledge, and prompt variance. From a pool of all qualifying text-based papers ∗ across ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, ACL, and EMNLP (2021–2025), most papers neither distinguish hallucination from uncertainty nor test prompt variance before considering external knowledge as a source. The methods that skip these distinctions risk targeting the wrong error type entirely. The detailed explanations are in § C . ∗ We did not filter papers further if they use the term “hallucination” in the title and take a text-based approach. We audit all the text-based papers with “hallucination” in the title from five major venues (2021–2025; § C ) and survey 24 of their first authors (§ B ). The paper categorization is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Two gaps stand out.

sections.heading: Hallucination is rarely separated from uncertainty.
sections.text: Only 35% of papers define hallucination as a confident or plausible error, and only 23% treat hallucination detection as distinct from uncertainty estimation. Yet 95.8% (23/24) of surveyed authors said the two should be distinguished; only 16.7% (4/24) said their own work did so.

sections.heading: Additional knowledge is added before cheaper inference-time mitigation methods are tried.
sections.text: Of papers concluding that external knowledge is needed (15% of the 91), most (11% of the 91) never tested whether the error disappears under a different phrasing, instruction or decoding setting. Survey respondents ranked knowledge availability, whether a model lacks a fact or misapplies it, as the most important dimension of hallucination (79.2%, 19/24). TAKEAWAY Most hallucination papers measure one undifferentiated error rate. They rarely separate confident incorrectness from expressed uncertainty, and rarely check whether the incorrect response survives rephrasing before adding knowledge, even though many authors think both distinctions matter.

sections.heading: 4 Terminology
sections.text: We hypothesize that incorrect responses fall into distinct error types, semantic illusion ( si ) and confabulation ( cf ), and that the distinction determines which detection and mitigation strategies apply. This section motivates both terms and defines them.

sections.heading: 4.1 Confabulations
sections.text: Confabulation classically refers to a systematic pattern of generating false narratives to bridge knowledge gaps while maintaining high confidence in the fabrications [ 65 , 83 ] . It is commonly used as a clinical term for verbal statements that are inconsistent with the patient’s history and current situation due to brain damage [ 7 , 66 , 48 , 6 , 28 ] . Consequently, confabulation can be associated with the absence of relevant memories in human cognition. While LLMs operate through fundamentally different mechanisms, they exhibit analogous patterns of generating false information. A hallucinated response is a confabulation if an LLM produces the incorrect output regardless of any inference-time changes. We hypothesize this is due to absent or inaccessible knowledge that is required by the input. Accordingly, we state that LLMs produce incorrect responses by confabulation when the pretrained knowledge or memory has limitations through two different mechanisms. One cause is the absence of necessary information in the training data. It is particularly evident when models with specific knowledge cut-off dates lack current information [ 16 , 103 ] . Such a phenomenon is known as absent memory or knowledge . Another cause occurs when relevant information exists in the training data but remains underlearned [ 63 , 76 ] . In these contexts, confabulation manifests as a persistent form of fabrication that resists correction through prompt engineering or inference-time hyperparameter tuning such as random seeds, temperatures, or top- p p distributions of the decoding mechanisms.

sections.heading: 4.2 Semantic Illusions
sections.text: We propose semantic illusion as a distinct type of hallucination, separate from confabulation. Unlike confabulation, semantic illusion occurs even though the relevant knowledge appears to be accessible in the model pretrained memory. The concept of semantic illusion is well-illustrated by the classic example in human cognition where individuals readily answer "two" when asked "how many animals of each kind did Moses take on the ark?", despite knowing that it was Noah who built the ark [ 26 , 10 ] . The illustration allows us to pinpoint two major features of semantic illusion: (1) we choose the erroneous answers even though we know the fact; (2) we can answer correctly under a different or even exactly the same phrasing. While the concept of semantic illusion has been studied in human cognition, it has not been formally defined or widely explored in the context of language models. Inspired by human cognitive illustration, we can define the following. A hallucinated response is a semantic illusion if an LLM produces an incorrect output despite being able to correctly answer the same or semantically equivalent inputs that require the same underlying factual knowledge, without any change to the model parameters (i.e., without further training). This phenomenon represents a behavioral analogue to human semantic illusions, wherein LLM generation is driven more by surface-level semantic compatibility than by factual knowledge encoded in the model. In particular, next-token prediction can be dominated by contextual associations that make an answer appear semantically appropriate within the immediate prompt, even when it conflicts with the correct underlying facts. By the autoregressive nature, language models fail to backtrack and reconsider the discrepancy from the semantic illusion, even though they later recognize that the current sequential generation is probabilistically suboptimal to find the correct information [ 116 , 107 ] . This is particularly pronounced in chain-of-thought reasoning, where detailed yet erroneous explanations appear consistently but deviate from accurate facts. It manifests through the model tendency to "snowball" incorrect information, elaborating on flawed premises to maintain the initial semantic coherence [ 111 ] .

sections.text: We evaluate 14 detection and mitigation methods from 2021–2025 (Table 1 ; See § F for detailed explanation and § F.1 for full design dimensions). sections.heading: The detection gap.
sections.text: Methods find cf harder to detect than si (Fig. 5 ). Across all methods, recall is similar under S1 (about 67% for both), but under S2, where uncertainty is elicited, cf recall drops by 13.6 points (to 53.4%) while si recall remains unchanged. cf is also left with much higher residual error than si . Overall, cf is missed more often and more persistently than si .

sections.heading: The mitigation gap.
sections.text: Across all mitigation methods, 28.5% (S1) and 29.6% (S2) of flagged si errors end up correct, against 0.7% and 2.8% of flagged cf errors (mitigation correctness in Fig. 5 ). In the rest of the paper, we show that the gap holds for two different model families, different labeling schemes, and almost every | 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) | |\mathcal{V}(Q)| from 1 to 30.

sections.heading: Where it comes from.
sections.text: Each intervention stage shows a distinct pattern (Fig. 6 ). Inference-time methods detect well but mitigate little; they can only redistribute probability over answers the model already produces, and a cf question has no correct answer to redistribute towards. Post-hoc methods flag incorrect responses including expressed uncertainty readily but mitigate almost nothing (slightly on si ). External-knowledge methods are the only intervention whose cf mitigation is clearly above zero, with little decline as | 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) | |\mathcal{V}(Q)| grows. Yet they do not discriminate between si , cf , and unk ; the methods flag them about equally often. Their mitigation effects ( si , then cf , then unk ) therefore do not follow need, and possibly reflect how much the external knowledge happens to help each type. Figure 6: Gaps by intervention stage , as | 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) | |\mathcal{V}(Q)| grows. Only external-knowledge methods (highlighted) mitigate cf well above zero (about 20%), while inference-time and post-hoc methods stay near zero. See § I.1 for further details on the gaps between cf and si , and § I.2 for further analysis of how each intervention type affects them. TAKEAWAY Existing methods mostly mitigate errors that a rephrasing would also fix. Before reaching for retrieval or retraining, test re-elicitation: if the error is si , cheap fixes work; if it is cf , only new knowledge does.

sections.heading: Uncertainty-based methods favor unk .
sections.text: Under both schemes, uncertainty-based methods give their highest mean score to unk (0.61 and 0.57), above cf (0.54, 0.42) and si (0.43, 0.42), and miss unk least often (Table 3 ; Fig. 1 c).

sections.heading: Uncertainty elicitation still does not help detect cf .
sections.text: Without uncertainty elicitation (S1), cf and si are detected at similar rates; cf is even missed slightly less often (34.2% vs. 35.6%). Uncertainty elicitation (S2) moves most cf into unk (the proportion of cf falls from 0.36 to 0.04; Table 2 ). The cf that remain are those the model asserts even when allowed to say “I don’t know”, and detectors miss half of them (50.4%). This clearly shows that the cf that remain are no easier to mitigate. TAKEAWAY A detector that scores “I don’t know” as its most likely hallucination is measuring expressed uncertainty ( unk ), not hallucination. Report unk separately; otherwise a method can look better simply by detecting uncertain responses, while missing the confidently incorrect responses ( si and cf ) that matter most. We refer readers to § I.3 for further details in uncertainty-based methods for hallucinations.

A cf answer contains no verbal cue to read. • Latent (internal-state) signals give the best cf detection among uncertainty representations, exceeding their own si detection at every | 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) | |\mathcal{V}(Q)| , and the most cf and unk mitigation among them. • Semantic (consistency-based) signals give the best si mitigation, as expected: inconsistency across samples is exactly what defines si . Verbal uncertainty methods suits expressed uncertainty, semantic consistency suits semantic illusions, and for confabulations, internal states are the only uncertainty signal we tested that shows a mitigation effect at a meaningful rate.

sections.heading: 10 Recommendations
sections.text: Based on our findings, we suggest four practical steps for hallucination research. First, define hallucination as confident incorrectness and explicitly distinguish it from expressed uncertainty, as conflating them risks targeting different phenomena under the same label. Second, report cf , si , and unk separately rather than aggregating all incorrect outputs, so that performance gains can be attributed to the right error type. Third, test semantically equivalent phrasings before introducing external knowledge : errors recoverable through rephrasing may not require retrieval augmentation, and this diagnostic can be often inexpensive relative to the interventions it can rule out. Fourth, match uncertainty representation to the target error type : verbal, latent, and semantic signals perform differently across each type, and latent representations are more promising than verbal ones for mitigating cf and unk . We hope these steps make hallucination evaluations more comparable across studies and help ensure that reported improvements reflect progress on the intended problem.

sections.heading: 11 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.text: Hallucination research currently lacks consistent operational distinctions across multiple error types. The term is applied inconsistently, and behaviorally different incorrect responses are often aggregated into a single metric. We decompose incorrect model outputs into three operational categories: confabulation ( cf ), semantic illusion ( si ), and expressed uncertainty ( unk ). Empirically, we show that cf remains substantially harder for existing methods to mitigate, and to detect under uncertainty elicitation, while si is often recoverable under inference-time intervention. Although our study covers a limited set of models, datasets, and methods, the si – cf mitigation gap holds across both models, both labeling schemes, and all variant-set sizes. Because cf is defined by persistent incorrectness under prompt variation, one might expect prompt-level methods to fail on cf by construction. This is not the case in our setup: 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{V}(Q) is used only for labeling, and evaluated methods operate on held-out prompts they never see during labeling. The gap also holds for methods that do not use paraphrasing at all, including inference-time decoding and latent-state methods (Fig. 15 c, 16 a), so the taxonomy predicts which interventions succeed rather than restating its definition. We propose that future work define hallucination precisely, disaggregate error types, and audit alignment between definitions and evaluation methods.

sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools for generating synthetic data, specifically the semantically equivalent question paraphrases that make up 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{V}(Q) , creating data visualization for our results, interpreting results, and refining and proof-reading the draft. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. Generated paraphrases were checked for semantic equivalence and for the absence of answer hints, and we further verified that they do not increase the likelihood of the gold answer. AI-assisted interpretations were verified by the authors against the underlying experimental results and all text edits were reviewed by the authors. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: Survey responses were collected from researchers who publish on LLM hallucinations. All responses were collected before respondents were informed of our hypotheses or taxonomy, to avoid biasing them. Participation was voluntary, all respondents agreed to the use of their responses, and only aggregate results are reported. All QA data come from publicly available benchmarks (TriviaQA, SimpleQA) and contain no private information. Call for contributions. We believe clarifying what hallucination benchmarks measure is a community effort. If you develop hallucination detection or mitigation methods and would like them evaluated under our taxonomy, or want to extend it to new settings, please get in touch: hazel.kim@cs.ox.ac.uk .

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: Definition Despite its widespread usage, the term hallucination lacks a consensus definition across the research community. The proportion of papers explicitly defining it has declined steadily since 2021 [ 68 ] . Early NLP usage anchored the term to faithfulness failures, describing generated content unfaithful to a provided source [ 45 , 117 ] . With the rise of LLMs, definitions have diverged along two axes. The first concerns the nature of incorrectness : from source unfaithfulness [ 45 , 117 ] , to real-world unfactualness covering fictional, misleading, or fabricated outputs [ 82 , 3 , 2 ] , and further to outputs conflicting with instructions, context, or logical consistency [ 12 , 39 ] . The second concerns the degree of plausibility : from outputs that simply appear fluent and coherent [ 2 , 3 ] , to those whose plausibility is treated as an unavoidable consequence of how LLMs generate text [ 114 , 53 ] , to the strictest view requiring misplaced confidence, restricting hallucination to assertions the model delivers with unwarranted certainty [ 47 , 68 , 39 ] . Terminology The terminological ambiguity has prompted calls for more precise alternatives. A systematic study of researcher perspectives [ 68 ] found that 40.46% prefer fabrication , while others advocate for confabulation , a clinical term for false narratives produced to bridge knowledge gaps without intent to deceive [ 7 , 65 , 83 ] . This preference reflects a broader concern that models frequently fabricate responses without sufficient grounds. The clinical origin of the term, however, is more specific, denoting errors arising from missing or inaccessible knowledge [ 7 , 65 , 83 , 16 , 63 ] . Under this view, responses may vary in form across semantically equivalent prompt variants, yet remain incorrect regardless of how the question is phrased. This captures only one error type. We therefore retain hallucination as the cover term and decompose it into two behaviorally distinct subtypes, confabulation and semantic illusion , whose empirically separable signatures we define in § E.1 and analyze in § I . Taxonomy Early survey work established the foundational intrinsic/extrinsic taxonomy, where intrinsic hallucinations contradict the source content and extrinsic hallucinations introduce unverifiable information [ 45 ] . Subsequent work expanded this line of taxonomies. [ 117 ] proposed input-conflicting, context-conflicting, and fact-conflicting categories to capture misaligned responses beyond source documents, while [ 39 , 95 ] separated factuality hallucination from faithfulness hallucination across a hierarchical set of subtypes. [ 3 ] attributed hallucinations to either prompting or model-internal factors by measuring how errors change across prompt variants and across models. Unlike prior taxonomies based on triggers or contradictions, we classify hallucinations by prompt sensitivity, distinguishing consistent incorrectness ( confabulation ) from prompt-sensitive incorrectness ( semantic illusion ), and linking each to corresponding detection and mitigation strategies.

sections.heading: Appendix B Author Survey
sections.text: We surveyed 24 first authors of hallucination papers published at top-tier ML/NLP venues, asking which dimensions matter most for categorizing hallucination (select all that apply). Responses were collected before respondents saw our hypotheses or taxonomy. Figure 8: Dimensions that 24 first authors of hallucination papers consider most important for categorizing hallucination. Each bar is the fraction of respondents who selected that dimension; multiple selections were allowed, so percentages do not sum to 100%. Dark bars mark the dimensions underlying our CF/SI/UNK taxonomy. As Figure 8 shows, the two most frequently selected dimensions are knowledge availability , whether the model lacks the relevant knowledge or misapplies knowledge it has (79.2%), and causal origin , whether the error arises from training data or from inference-time dynamics (75.0%). These are the axes along which our taxonomy separates hallucinations (Section 5 ), so most researchers independently favor the same distinctions. Dimensions concerning the knowledge source, error type, and prompt sensitivity form a middle tier (41.0–50.0%), while those describing the setting rather than the cause of an error, namely task type, input modality, and multimodality, were rarely selected (8.3–16.7%). Researchers thus view why a model hallucinates, rather than where , as the more useful basis for categorization.

sections.heading: Appendix C What the Community Measures
sections.text: Recent hallucination-titled papers reveal two systematic methodological gaps (Fig. 9 ). The first is the hallucination-uncertainty 4 4 4 Note that uncertainty here encompasses both expressed uncertainty and uncertainty estimation methods, which are treated as distinct concepts throughout the paper. distinction in definitions and methodologies. Only 35% of papers nominally define hallucination as confident or plausible errors rather than expressed uncertainty , and even this is not always reflected in methodology. While 23% treat hallucination detection as distinct from uncertainty estimation 5 5 5 Methods that quantify epistemic uncertainty in model outputs, e.g., via token probabilities. , not all anchor this in a confidence-based definition. Researchers broadly agree this distinction matters, as confirmed by a survey of 24 first authors of hallucination papers in top ML/NLP venues. 95.8% believe hallucination should be distinguished from uncertainty (both expressed and estimated), yet only 16.7% report treating them as distinct in their work. We address this mismatch, a gap whose practical consequences we define in § E.2 and quantify in § I.3 . Figure 9: Recent text-based hallucination papers filtered by their definitions and approaches with uncertainty estimation, additional knowledge, and prompt variance. From a pool of qualifying text-based papers ∗ across ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, ACL, and EMNLP (2021–2025), most papers neither distinguish hallucination from uncertainty nor test prompt variance before considering external knowledge as a source. The methods that skip these distinctions risk targeting the wrong error type entirely. Table 4 lists the papers with their category at each stage, and Table 5 groups the paper IDs by category. ∗ We did not filter papers further if they use the term “hallucination” in the title and take a text-based approach. The second gap is knowledge diagnosis. Among papers engaging with hallucination and uncertainty, those concluding that new external knowledge is necessary (15% of total) mostly never tested prompt variance first (11% of total), despite many incorrect responses yielding correct ones under different question phrasings, instruction prompts, or inference-time decoding configurations (§ A and § E.1 ). Among those that do not introduce new knowledge (19% of total), some never tested prompt variance either (3% of total papers), potentially leaving their results suboptimal when simple prompt interventions could yield further gains. Without these diagnostics, methods risk over-engineering solutions to errors that simpler interventions would resolve. This concern is crucial in hallucination research with 79.2% of surveyed researchers identifying knowledge availability, whether a model lacks knowledge versus misapplies it, as the most critical dimension for characterizing hallucinations (Fig. 8 ). We surveyed the 91 text-based papers in our literature (Tables 4 and 5 ) for the Figure 9 . Definition (“How does the paper define hallucination?”): confident error (“confident, factually incorrect output”; 35%), any factual error (“any factually incorrect output, regardless of expressed confidence”; 40%), unfaithful output (“output unfaithful to the provided context or document”; 21%), or inconsistent output (“output logically inconsistent within a single response”; 4%). Only the first two continue through the funnel. Uncertainty (“Does the paper distinguish hallucination from uncertainty?”): acknowledged/distinct if the paper answers “yes, they are fundamentally different phenomena” or “partially, acknowledged but not operationalized”; used as proxy if it answers “no, it uses uncertainty signals as proxies”; and uniform treatment if it answers “no, it treats all incorrect outputs uniformly”. Of the 91 papers, 23% are acknowledged/distinct, 11% are used as proxy, and 66% fall in the gray flow, which merges uniform treatment with papers whose definition fails the first filter. New knowledge (“Are errors reducible without new knowledge?”): no new knowledge if the paper reduces errors without new knowledge (19%), and needs knowledge if it requires external knowledge or retraining, or only partially fixes errors without it (15%). Prompt variance (“Do errors persist across reformulations of the prompt?”): tested if the paper reports that errors are stable, disappear, or are mixed across paraphrases (18%), and not tested if it does not test this or the question is not applicable (16%). The last two stages are followed only for the 31 papers (34%) that pass both of the first two filters. sections.heading: Appendix D Motivation for the Terminology
sections.text: We categorize hallucinated responses into two qualitatively different subtypes: confabulation and semantic illusion . In this section, we explain where each term comes from and why it fits the corresponding error type.

sections.heading: Type#1: Confabulation
sections.text: Confabulation classically refers to a systematic pattern of generating false narratives to bridge knowledge gaps while maintaining high confidence in the fabrications [ 65 , 83 ] . It is commonly used as a clinical term for verbal statements that are inconsistent with the patient’s history and current situation due to brain damage [ 7 , 66 , 48 , 6 , 28 ] . Consequently, confabulation can be associated with the absence of relevant memories in human cognition. While LLMs operate through fundamentally different mechanisms, they exhibit analogous patterns of generating false information. A hallucinated response is a confabulation if an LLM produces the incorrect output regardless of any inference-time changes. We hypothesize this is due to absent or inaccessible memory relevant to the factual information required by the input. Accordingly, we state that LLMs produce incorrect responses by confabulation when the memory has limitations through two different mechanisms. One cause is the absence of necessary information in the training data. It is particularly evident when models with specific knowledge cut-off dates lack current information [ 16 , 103 ] . Such a phenomenon is known as absent memory . Another cause occurs when relevant information exists in the training data but remains underlearned [ 63 , 76 ] . In these contexts, confabulation manifests as a persistent form of fabrication that resists correction through prompt engineering or inference-time hyperparameter tuning such as random seeds, temperatures, or top- p p distributions of the decoding mechanisms.

sections.heading: Type#2: Semantic Illusion
sections.text: We propose semantic illusion as a distinct type of hallucination, separate from confabulation. Unlike confabulation, semantic illusion occurs even if the eligible memory has the relevant information. It is well-illustrated by the classic example in human cognition where individuals readily answer "two" when asked "how many animals of each kind did Moses take on the ark?", despite knowing that it was Noah who built the ark [ 26 , 10 ] . The illustration allows us to pinpoint the two major features of semantic illusion: (1) we choose the erroneous answers even though we know the fact; (2) we do not capture the semantic oddness since the words within the question and answer seem to get along well with each other. While the concept of semantic illusion has been studied in human cognition, it has not been formally defined or widely explored in the context of language models. Inspired by human cognitive illustration, we can define the following. A hallucinated response is a semantic illusion if an LLM produces an incorrect output despite being able to correctly answer the same or semantically equivalent inputs that require the same underlying factual knowledge, without any change to the model parameters (i.e., without further training). This phenomenon represents a behavioral analogue to human semantic illusions, wherein LLM generation is driven more by surface-level semantic compatibility than by factual knowledge encoded in the model. In particular, next-token prediction can be dominated by contextual associations that make an answer appear semantically appropriate within the immediate prompt, even when it conflicts with the correct underlying facts. By the autoregressive nature, language models fail to backtrack and reconsider the discrepancy from the semantic illusion, even though they later recognize that the current sequential generation is probabilistically suboptimal to find the correct information [ 116 , 107 ] . This is particularly pronounced in chain-of-thought reasoning, where detailed yet erroneous explanations appear consistently but deviate from accurate facts. It manifests through the model tendency to "snowball" incorrect information, elaborating on flawed premises to maintain the initial semantic coherence [ 111 ] .

sections.heading: Appendix E Problem Formulation
sections.text: We formalize the two central hallucination dimensions – incorrectness and plausibility – through the following research questions (RQ) and hypotheses (H).

sections.heading: E.1 RQ1 (Incorrectness): Do hallucinations arise from distinct error types?
E.2 RQ2 (Plausibility): Does hallucination require confident incorrectness?
sections.text: We define plausibility as confidence, because (i) current LLMs are fluent by default, so surface plausibility is satisfied by nearly every output and draws no useful boundary, and (ii) a confidently stated incorrect response gives the reader no cue to check it, which makes it the more dangerous error. We say a response is confident if it does not explicitly express uncertainty. A confidently incorrect response ( cf , si ) and an expressed uncertainty ( unk ) may both be scored as incorrect, but reflect qualitatively different behaviors and risks. Uncertainty estimation methods were originally developed to quantify epistemic uncertainty as a signal for detecting incorrect outputs, whereas unk is a behavior in which the model explicitly abstains. As LLMs increasingly exhibit this behavior, the remaining errors are predominantly confident ones, where output-level uncertainty signals have least to detect. We ask whether confidence is a necessary condition for hallucination and whether existing methods respect this distinction in practice. Definition 3 Expressed Uncertainty ( unk ) A response to question Q Q is an expressed uncertainty if the model produces an incorrect answer on every variant in 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{V}(Q) but abstains on at least one. H3 (Uncertainty asymmetry). If detection methods conflate unk with hallucination, they will assign higher hallucination scores to unk than to cf and si , flagging the less dangerous error type more readily than the more dangerous ones. H4 (Representation asymmetry). Among uncertainty-based methods, verbal representations will be most effective at detecting unk , which carries an explicit uncertainty cue in its output. In contrast, cf carries no such cue. Therefore, latent representations, which read internal states beyond the output, will be most effective at detecting and mitigating cf .

sections.heading: Prompt sensitivity
sections.text: A method models prompt sensitivity if it explicitly evaluates how responses vary across semantically equivalent prompt variants 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{V}(Q) . Methods testing on a single prompt do not model this variation.

sections.heading: Intervention stage
sections.text: We distinguish three points where a method can intervene: during generation ( inference ), after generation ( post-hoc ), or by augmenting the model capabilities with external knowledge .

sections.heading: Knowledge assumption
sections.text: A method either assumes the correct knowledge exists in the model but is misapplied, pointing to a retrieval failure ( present knowledge ), or assumes the knowledge is absent entirely and must be supplied through external sources (i.e., external knowledge), pointing to a knowledge gap ( absent knowledge ).

sections.heading: Uncertainty usage
sections.text: Uncertainty signals can serve two purposes, either (i) estimating how likely a response is to be correct ( calibration ), or (ii) actively modifying outputs based on that signal ( correction )

sections.heading: Uncertainty representation
sections.text: A method may capture, express, or quantify uncertainty through expressed uncertainty in outputs ( verbal ), internal model states ( latent ), consistency across multiple outputs ( semantic ), or not engage with uncertainty at all ( none ).

sections.heading: Target error
sections.text: Each method primarily targets an error type from our taxonomy: semantic illusion , addressed through prompt sensitivity modeling; confabulation , addressed through knowledge augmentation; or expressed uncertainty , addressed through verbal uncertainty signals.

sections.heading: Appendix G Dataset Construction
sections.text: This appendix provides the complete dataset construction pipeline, including prompt templates, behavioral grid specification, and labeling criteria. The main paper (§ 6 ) summarizes the design; this appendix provides the detail needed for replication. We construct a controlled factual QA dataset drawn from TriviaQA [ 49 ] and SimpleQA [ 101 ] across ( nh , si , cf , unk ) categories for our study. We study closed-book factual question answering, because it provides verifiable ground truth, makes model knowledge the sole explanatory variable, and removes retrieval or grounding confounds. We assign them by 30 semantically equivalent question variants for a practical evaluation. We report all main results across two different instruction methods (see details in § G ). S1 applies a richer grid of 30 semantically equivalent variants, 3 instruction prompts without uncertainty elicitation, and multiple inference-time decoding configurations (e.g., temperatures, see details in § G.3 ); S2 additionally includes an uncertainty-elicitation instruction.

sections.heading: G.1 Source Datasets
sections.text: Candidate questions are drawn from two publicly available factual QA benchmarks: • TriviaQA [ 49 ] : open-domain trivia questions with verified answers. We use the unfiltered development split and restrict to questions with short-phrase answers to ensure unambiguous correctness evaluation. • SimpleQA [ 101 ] : a benchmark specifically designed to probe factual knowledge with short, verifiable questions and a structured confidence-elicitation protocol. We adopt SimpleQA’s calibration prompt (see § G.2 ). We apply the following pre-filters before behavioral evaluation: (i) answers must be short and unambiguous (no date ranges, no “either X or Y” answers); (ii) questions must not require world-knowledge updated after the training cutoff of any construction model for semantic illusion type. The remaining pool of candidates is passed to the behavioral evaluation grid described in § G.3 .

sections.heading: G.2 Confidence Prompt Template
sections.text: All responses during construction and evaluation are elicited using the following prompt, adapted directly from SimpleQA’s calibration method: Confidence Prompt (used for all models) Here is the question: {question} Please provide your best guess and a confidence score between 0% to 100% in the following JSON format: { "answer": "Your answer here", "confidence_score": number } We observe that under this prompt, models across families consistently assign high confidence to incorrect responses (Figure 11 ). When models explicitly state that they do not know or refuse to answer, their confidence scores are almost always near zero [ 101 ] . The confidence score therefore adds little information beyond the verbal expression of uncertainty. Figure 11: Model confidence scores across different response categories – correct/incorrect responses and not attempted – on the TriviaQA validation split (5k) and SimpleQA (4.3k). High confidence on incorrect responses and near-zero confidence on not-attempted responses show that the confidence score is consistent with explicit verbal uncertainty.

sections.heading: G.3 Behavioral Evaluation
sections.text: Each candidate questions per category nh , si , cf , and unk are evaluated under a dense behavioral grid designed to probe response stability across input perturbations that are semantically equivalent but surface-form variable.

sections.heading: Instruction variants.
sections.text: We evaluate each question under 4 instruction prompt variants that vary the framing of the task. Each instruction variant is crossed with each perturbation condition. Instruction Prompt Variants 1 Answer the question with a short factual phrase. Output only the answer. 2 Return a concise answer only. No explanation. 3 Provide only the entity/date/name that answers the question. 4 Give the most likely factual answer. If uncertain, say: I don’t know. (uncertainty-elicitation)

sections.heading: Inference-time decoding configurations.
sections.text: We evaluate each (question, condition, instruction) triple under multiple decoding settings: greedy decoding, temperature sampling ( T ∈ { 0.2 , 0.7 } T\in\{0.2,0.7\} ), and nucleus sampling ( p = 0.80 , 0.95 p=0.80,0.95 ). This ensures that behavioral labels are not artifacts of a single decoding strategy.

sections.heading: Semantic paraphrase variants.
sections.text: We additionally evaluate each question under 30 semantically equivalent paraphrases that vary linguistic structure and lexical choices without adding hints or information.

Uncertainty estimation detects unk best but mitigates only si (Table 8 ). Detection methods assign higher hallucination scores to unk than to si and cf . This means that the hallucination detection methods strongly align with the unk responses, consistently stronger than the cf regardless of the uncertainty elicitation setting (i.e., both S1 and S2 labeling schemes). The gap arises as the uncertainty based methods rely on uncertainty cues, which cf responses do not carry due to their confident incorrectness. Output-level signals are well-suited to unk while latent representations are promising for cf (Fig. 16(a) ). Verbal (output-level) uncertainty achieves the best detection on unk among uncertainty representations, while showing the worst detection on cf . Latent representations achieve the best detection on cf among uncertainty representations, better than si across all | 𝒱 ⁡ ( 𝒬 ) | |\mathcal{V(Q)}| . The favorable patterns of latent methods hold in mitigation. Among the uncertainty representations, latent methods mitigate the most cf and unk responses. The advantage of using verbal representation does not translate to mitigation effect, however. Instead, semantic representation shows the best mitigation correctness on si . Methods in the None group mitigate cf even better than latent methods, but they rely on external knowledge or decoding instead of uncertainty. Correction methods mitigate cf and unk slightly better than calibration methods (Fig. 16(b) ). Mitigation methods that use uncertainty to correct the original response, achieve slightly higher mitigation effect on cf and unk than Calibration methods, which use uncertainty primarily as a scoring signal. Mitigation methods therefore represent a promising step beyond calibration, yielding measurable gains in cf and unk mitigation. However, these gains remain modest relative to their near ceiling detection of si , cf , and unk , leaving substantial room to translate successful detection into correct answers.

Kim 1,∗ Jakub Binkowski 2 Ekaterina Fadeeva 3 Juan David Guerra 4,5 Yijie Hao 6 Zheng Yi Ho 7 Baixiang Huang 6 Buyun Liang 8 Siyuan Liang 7 Anh Tuan Luu 9 Potsawee Manakul 10 Niels Mündler-Sasahara 3 Aidar Myrzakhan 11 Shahrad Mohammadzadeh 12 Artem Shelmanov 11 Kai Shu 6 Ponhvoan Srey 7 Dacheng Tao 7 René Vidal 8 Haofei Yu 13 Lei Yu 14,15 Hongxiang Zhang 16 Yarin Gal 1 Hinrich Schütze 17 Philip H.S. Torr 1 1 University of Oxford 2 Wroclaw University of Science and Technology 3 ETH Zurich 4 Mila – Quebec AI Institute 5 Polytechnique Montréal 6 Emory University 7 Nanyang Technological University 8 University of Pennsylvania 9 VinUniversity 10 Independent Researcher 11 MBZUAI 12 McGill University 13 UIUC 14 University of Toronto 15 Meta (FAIR) 16 Purdue University 17 LMU Munich * Correspondence to hazel.kim@cs.ox.ac.uk Abstract Hallucination remains one of the most critical challenges in deploying large language models (LLMs) reliably and safely. Yet the term is used inconsistently across the research community. We argue for a strict definition of hallucinations in LLMs. First, hallucinations should be confident incorrectness , kept separate from expressed uncertainty ( unk ) 1 1 1 Model responses that explicitly communicate epistemic uncertainty, including both abstention (i.e., declining to provide an answer) and low-confidence answers (e.g., ”I am not sure but maybe …”, ”I don’t know but …”). . unk reveals that the model may be wrong, whereas a hallucination does not reveal it and is therefore more dangerous in practice. Conflating the two obscures their distinct behaviors and makes them hard to study. Second, hallucinations should be split by a simple re-elicitation test: does any semantically equivalent prompt recover the correct response? This test probes whether the relevant knowledge 2 2 2 We use knowledge loosely to mean relevant information stored in the model’s latent representations (i.e., pretrained, parametric knowledge). Whether a model truly possesses a piece of knowledge cannot be verified from the outside: it may be stored but unretrievable, or absent from training. We therefore operationally treat knowledge as accessible if some semantically equivalent prompt elicits it without model parameter changes. is accessible. If none does, the knowledge is likely absent or inaccessible, and the error type is a confabulation ( cf ) that likely requires external knowledge or retraining; if some does, the knowledge is accessible from the model but applied inconsistently, and the error type is a semantic illusion ( si ) that simple prompt or decoding changes can mitigate 3 3 3 Any intervention that revises an originally incorrect model response into a correct one. . Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods under this taxonomy yields three findings. (1) Detection methods flag unk more often than hallucinated responses (i.e., si and cf ). (2) Mitigation methods are far more effective for si than for cf . (3) Latent signals are more informative than output-level signals for cf . An audit of recent hallucination papers shows that most conflate these categories. We recommend reporting cf , si , and unk separately, and introduce a practical labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of semantically equivalent prompts. 1 Introduction Original prompt answered correctly? Any re-elicitation answered correctly? Expresses uncertainty under any condition? No hallucination correct under the original prompt Semantic illusion hallucination, recoverable Expressed uncertainty admits it is unsure; not a hallucination Confabulation hallucination, unrecoverable yes yes yes no no no Re-elicitation: paraphrase, instruction or decoding change (without additional information) Figure 1: Proposed taxonomy of model responses. An incorrect answer is a semantic illusion if any semantically equivalent re-elicitation recovers the correct answer. If none does, it is a confabulation, unless the model expresses uncertainty under some condition, in which case it is unk . Only si and cf are hallucinations. Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a central concern for both researchers and practitioners. Yet there is surprisingly little consensus on what the term actually means. Across the literature, it is applied to a broad and heterogeneous set of model failures—factual inaccuracies [ 82 , 3 , 2 ] , faithfulness errors [ 45 , 117 ] , reasoning inconsistencies [ 39 , 12 ] , and uncertain outputs [ 117 , 39 , 102 ] —often without distinction or explicit definition. This conceptual ambiguity is not merely terminological but obscures the underlying causes of model incorrect responses, undermines evaluation validity, and hinders the development of targeted mitigation strategies. We propose one definition and one test (Fig. 1 ). A hallucination is a confident incorrect response, so a model that says “I don’t know” is expressing uncertainty ( unk ), not hallucinating. Hallucinations then split by whether the knowledge is behaviorally accessible . If some paraphrase, instruction or decoding setting recovers the correct answer, the error is a semantic illusion ( si ); if none does, it is a confabulation ( cf ) (see § 4 for terminological motivations). The test is an operational proxy for knowledge accessibility, and it makes a sharp prediction that si should yield to inexpensive inference-time mitigation, while cf should need new, additional knowledge. Our main contributions and findings are as follows: • An audit of the community (§ 3 ). Only 35% of recent hallucination papers define hallucination as confident incorrectness. Yet 95.8% of surveyed first authors say it should be distinguished from uncertainty, and only 16.7% report that they did so. • A behavioral taxonomy (§ 5 ) We define hallucination as a confidently incorrect response, separate from expressed uncertainty ( unk ), and introduce two error types based on a re-elicitation test: semantic illusions ( si ), which some semantically equivalent re-elicitation corrects, and confabulations ( cf ), which none does. We use this taxonomy to re-evaluate 14 hallucination methods on two LLMs. • Mitigation for semantic illusions, not for confabulations (§ 7 ). Methods mitigate 28–29% of detected si responses but 0.7–2.8% of cf responses; only external knowledge improves cf mitigation, to about 20%. • Uncertainty-based detectors mostly measure expressed uncertainty (§ 8 ). They give their highest scores to unk , which is not a hallucination, above both si and cf , and they miss half of the cf responses that remain once uncertainty is elicited. • The right uncertainty representation depends on the error type (§ 9 ). Among uncertainty representations, verbal ones detect unk best but barely mitigate it; latent ones detect and mitigate cf best; and semantic ones mitigate si best. These effects are invisible in an aggregate hallucination score. An audit of recent papers (§ 3 and § B ) shows such aggregation is the norm. We also contribute a labeling protocol (§ 5 ) that stabilizes at about ten paraphrases, so the taxonomy is plausible to adopt. 2 Problem Formulation We formalize the two central hallucination dimensions – incorrectness and plausibility – through the following research questions (RQ). The detailed hypotheses (H) are illustrated in § E . 2.1 RQ1 (Incorrectness): Do hallucinations arise from distinct error types? The most basic condition for hallucinations is incorrectness, whether measured against a source [ 45 , 117 ] , the real-world facts [ 82 , 3 , 2 ] , or an instruction [ 39 , 12 ] . Incorrect outputs, however, are not uniform in how they arise or how they respond to elicitation. Accordingly, the difference that matters most in practice is consistency of occurrence. Yet some incorrect responses can be corrected under a semantically equivalent phrasing ( semantic illusion ), while others recur whatever phrasing is used ( confabulation ) (see § 4 or § D for an explanation of the terminology). We ask whether these reflect distinct error types, and whether that distinction changes which detection and mitigation strategies apply. The difference also invites an epistemic reading, since a response that becomes correct under a semantically equivalent phrasing shows the relevant knowledge is accessible without changing model weights or injecting additional information. We therefore treat knowledge as behaviorally accessible when some tested condition elicits a correct response. The conditions we admit that establish accessibility are semantically equivalent phrasings, instruction variants, decoding configurations (e.g., temperature, nucleus sampling), which require no access to model internals and add no additional hints or context. 2.2 RQ2 (Plausibility): Does hallucination require confident incorrectness? We define plausibility as confidence, because (i) current LLMs are fluent by default, so surface plausibility is satisfied by nearly every output and draws no useful boundary, and (ii) a confidently stated incorrect response gives the reader no cue to check it, which makes it the more dangerous error. We say a response is confident if it does not explicitly express uncertainty. A confidently incorrect response ( cf , si ) and an expressed uncertainty ( unk ) may both be scored as incorrect, but reflect qualitatively different behaviors and risks. Uncertainty estimation methods were originally developed to quantify epistemic uncertainty as a signal for detecting incorrect outputs, whereas unk is a behavior in which the model explicitly abstains or gives a low-confidence answer. As LLMs increasingly exhibit this behavior, the remaining errors are predominantly confident ones, where output-level uncertainty signals have least to detect. We ask whether confidence is a necessary condition for hallucination and whether existing methods respect this distinction in practice. 3 What the Community Measures Figure 2: Recent text-based hallucination papers filtered by their definitions and approaches with uncertainty estimation, additional knowledge, and prompt variance. From a pool of all qualifying text-based papers ∗ across ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, ACL, and EMNLP (2021–2025), most papers neither distinguish hallucination from uncertainty nor test prompt variance before considering external knowledge as a source. The methods that skip these distinctions risk targeting the wrong error type entirely. The detailed explanations are in § C . ∗ We did not filter papers further if they use the term “hallucination” in the title and take a text-based approach. We audit all the text-based papers with “hallucination” in the title from five major venues (2021–2025; § C ) and survey 24 of their first authors (§ B ). The paper categorization is illustrated in Fig. 2 . Two gaps stand out. Hallucination is rarely separated from uncertainty. Only 35% of papers define hallucination as a confident or plausible error, and only 23% treat hallucination detection as distinct from uncertainty estimation. Yet 95.8% (23/24) of surveyed authors said the two should be distinguished; only 16.7% (4/24) said their own work did so. Additional knowledge is added before cheaper inference-time mitigation methods are tried. Of papers concluding that external knowledge is needed (15% of the 91), most (11% of the 91) never tested whether the error disappears under a different phrasing, instruction or decoding setting. Survey respondents ranked knowledge availability, whether a model lacks a fact or misapplies it, as the most important dimension of hallucination (79.2%, 19/24). TAKEAWAY Most hallucination papers measure one undifferentiated error rate. They rarely separate confident incorrectness from expressed uncertainty, and rarely check whether the incorrect response survives rephrasing before adding knowledge, even though many authors think both distinctions matter. 4 Terminology We hypothesize that incorrect responses fall into distinct error types, semantic illusion ( si ) and confabulation ( cf ), and that the distinction determines which detection and mitigation strategies apply. This section motivates both terms and defines them. 4.1 Confabulations Confabulation classically refers to a systematic pattern of generating false narratives to bridge knowledge gaps while maintaining high confidence in the fabrications [ 65 , 83 ] . It is commonly used as a clinical term for verbal statements that are inconsistent with the patient’s history and current situation due to brain damage [ 7 , 66 , 48 , 6 , 28 ] . Consequently, confabulation can be associated with the absence of relevant memories in human cognition. While LLMs operate through fundamentally different mechanisms, they exhibit analogous patterns of generating false information. A hallucinated response is a confabulation if an LLM produces the incorrect output regardless of any inference-time changes. We hypothesize this is due to absent or inaccessible knowledge that is required by the input. Accordingly, we state that LLMs produce incorrect responses by confabulation when the pretrained knowledge or memory has limitations through two different mechanisms. One cause is the absence of necessary information in the training data. It is particularly evident when models with specific knowledge cut-off dates lack current information [ 16 , 103 ] . Such a phenomenon is known as absent memory or knowledge . Another cause occurs when relevant information exists in the training data but remains underlearned [ 63 , 76 ] . In these contexts, confabulation manifests as a persistent form of fabrication that resists correction through prompt engineering or inference-time hyperparameter tuning such as random seeds, temperatures, or top- p p distributions of the decoding mechanisms. 4.2 Semantic Illusions We propose semantic illusion as a distinct type of hallucination, separate from confabulation. Unlike confabulation, semantic illusion occurs even though the relevant knowledge appears to be accessible in the model pretrained memory. The concept of semantic illusion is well-illustrated by the classic example in human cognition where individuals readily answer "two" when asked "how many animals of each kind did Moses take on the ark?", despite knowing that it was Noah who built the ark [ 26 , 10 ] . The illustration allows us to pinpoint two major features of semantic illusion: (1) we choose the erroneous answers even though we know the fact; (2) we can answer correctly under a different or even exactly the same phrasing. While the concept of semantic illusion has been studied in human cognition, it has not been formally defined or widely explored in the context of language models. Inspired by human cognitive illustration, we can define the following. A hallucinated response is a semantic illusion if an LLM produces an incorrect output despite being able to correctly answer the same or semantically equivalent inputs that require the same underlying factual knowledge, without any change to the model parameters (i.e., without further training). This phenomenon represents a behavioral analogue to human semantic illusions, wherein LLM generation is driven more by surface-level semantic compatibility than by factual knowledge encoded in the model. In particular, next-token prediction can be dominated by contextual associations that make an answer appear semantically appropriate within the immediate prompt, even when it conflicts with the correct underlying facts. By the autoregressive nature, language models fail to backtrack and reconsider the discrepancy from the semantic illusion, even though they later recognize that the current sequential generation is probabilistically suboptimal to find the correct information [ 116 , 107 ] . This is particularly pronounced in chain-of-thought reasoning, where detailed yet erroneous explanations appear consistently but deviate from accurate facts. It manifests through the model tendency to "snowball" incorrect information, elaborating on flawed premises to maintain the initial semantic coherence [ 111 ] . 5 A Behavioral Taxonomy of Incorrect Responses 5.1 Definitions Fix a model M M and a question Q Q with gold answer A A . Grouping uncertainty-based methods by where they read uncertainty from (Fig. 7 ): • Verbal (output-level) signals give the best unk detection and the worst cf detection. A cf answer contains no verbal cue to read. • Latent (internal-state) signals give the best cf detection among uncertainty representations, exceeding their own si detection at every | 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) | |\mathcal{V}(Q)| , and the most cf and unk mitigation among them. • Semantic (consistency-based) signals give the best si mitigation, as expected: inconsistency across samples is exactly what defines si . Two caveats bound this claim. Methods that use no uncertainty at all mitigate cf better still, because that group contains the external-knowledge methods. Detailed analysis is in § I.3 . TAKEAWAY Match the signal to the error. Verbal uncertainty methods suits expressed uncertainty, semantic consistency suits semantic illusions, and for confabulations, internal states are the only uncertainty signal we tested that shows a mitigation effect at a meaningful rate. 10 Recommendations Based on our findings, we suggest four practical steps for hallucination research. First, define hallucination as confident incorrectness and explicitly distinguish it from expressed uncertainty, as conflating them risks targeting different phenomena under the same label. Second, report cf , si , and unk separately rather than aggregating all incorrect outputs, so that performance gains can be attributed to the right error type. Third, test semantically equivalent phrasings before introducing external knowledge : errors recoverable through rephrasing may not require retrieval augmentation, and this diagnostic can be often inexpensive relative to the interventions it can rule out. Fourth, match uncertainty representation to the target error type : verbal, latent, and semantic signals perform differently across each type, and latent representations are more promising than verbal ones for mitigating cf and unk . We hope these steps make hallucination evaluations more comparable across studies and help ensure that reported improvements reflect progress on the intended problem. 11 Limitations and Conclusion Hallucination research currently lacks consistent operational distinctions across multiple error types. The term is applied inconsistently, and behaviorally different incorrect responses are often aggregated into a single metric. We decompose incorrect model outputs into three operational categories: confabulation ( cf ), semantic illusion ( si ), and expressed uncertainty ( unk ). Empirically, we show that cf remains substantially harder for existing methods to mitigate, and to detect under uncertainty elicitation, while si is often recoverable under inference-time intervention. Although our study covers a limited set of models, datasets, and methods, the si – cf mitigation gap holds across both models, both labeling schemes, and all variant-set sizes. Because cf is defined by persistent incorrectness under prompt variation, one might expect prompt-level methods to fail on cf by construction. This is not the case in our setup: 𝒱 ⁡ ( Q ) \mathcal{V}(Q) is used only for labeling, and evaluated methods operate on held-out prompts they never see during labeling. The gap also holds for methods that do not use paraphrasing at all, including inference-time decoding and latent-state methods (Fig. 15 c, 16 a), so the taxonomy predicts which interventions succeed rather than restating its definition. We propose that future work define hallucination precisely, disaggregate error types, and audit alignment between definitions and evaluation methods.
